proposition: It is sometimes right to lie to someone for their own good.
cheap: Pointing at one emergency and stopping there. The hard part is stating the rule that lets you do it here and not everywhere.

proposition: Punishment is justified only by its future effects, never by desert.
cheap: Saying revenge is primitive. That is a sentiment, not an argument, and it does not address the intuition that the guilty deserve something.

proposition: You are as obliged to a stranger dying far away as to one dying in front of you.
cheap: Asserting that distance is morally arbitrary and leaving it there. The objection is that obligations track relationships, and you have to meet it.

proposition: The interests of an animal count the same as the equivalent interests of a human.
cheap: Comparing intelligence. That argument cuts against you the moment you apply it between humans.

proposition: Large inheritances should not be permitted.
cheap: Calling it unearned. Most advantages are unearned, including talent, so you need more than that.

proposition: A society should tolerate speech it believes to be false and harmful.
cheap: Quoting Mill and stopping. You have to answer the case where the speech demonstrably causes the harm.

proposition: Complete honesty with the people closest to you is a mistake.
cheap: Citing one white lie about a haircut. The hard version concerns things that matter.

proposition: You owe nothing in particular to the country you happened to be born in.
cheap: Saying borders are arbitrary. Families are arbitrary too, and few think that dissolves the obligation.

proposition: A drunk driver who kills someone is no more blameworthy than one who gets home safely.
cheap: Saying the outcome was luck. Our whole legal and moral practice disagrees, and you must explain why it is wrong rather than merely inconsistent.

proposition: People who do not yet exist have claims on us now.
cheap: Gesturing at the climate. That assumes what you are trying to prove.

proposition: Believing something without sufficient evidence is always wrong.
cheap: Quoting Clifford's shipowner. James answered it directly and you have to answer him.

proposition: On a technical question outside your competence you should defer to expert consensus even when the argument against it seems good to you.
cheap: Listing cases where experts were right. You need to handle the cases where they were wrong and the dissenters were right.

proposition: Moral intuitions are evidence, not just feelings to be explained away.
cheap: Saying everyone shares them. Plenty of discarded intuitions were widely shared.

proposition: There are truths that science is in principle unable to establish.
cheap: Naming consciousness and stopping. That is a hard problem, not a proof of impossibility.

proposition: Most of what you know, you know only because someone told you.
cheap: Listing facts you were taught. The interesting question is whether that counts as knowing.

proposition: You should hold no belief with complete certainty.
cheap: Saying we have been wrong before. Apply the claim to itself and see what happens.

proposition: Democracy is justified by something other than the quality of its decisions.
cheap: Saying voting feels fair. If the outcomes were consistently terrible, would you still say it?

proposition: A representative should vote their own judgment rather than their constituents' wishes.
cheap: Quoting Burke. State why the voters should accept it, in their terms.

proposition: Inequality of outcome matters in itself, not only because of what it does to the badly off.
cheap: Saying it feels unfair. Levelling down makes nobody better off, so you have to say why it is still an improvement.

proposition: The state may sometimes stop competent adults from harming only themselves.
cheap: Naming seatbelts. Mill's answer is that this concerns others too, so pick a purer case.

proposition: A country has the right to exclude people who want to move there.
cheap: Appealing to sovereignty. That restates the claim rather than defending it.

proposition: There is no duty to vote, because a single vote never decides anything.
cheap: The arithmetic alone. The obvious reply is that the same reasoning excuses everyone.

proposition: A practice surviving a long time is evidence that it is worth keeping.
cheap: Calling it wisdom. Slavery survived a long time too.

proposition: There are circumstances in which political violence is justified.
cheap: Naming an obvious tyranny. The hard part is the rule that stops it justifying far more.

proposition: Most people would be worse off, not better, if they did not have to work.
cheap: Citing lottery winners. Selection effects ruin that evidence.

proposition: A life of contentment is not obviously better than a difficult life spent on something that mattered.
cheap: Asserting that meaning beats pleasure. Say what makes meaning good if not, ultimately, how it feels.

proposition: Ambition does more harm than good to the person who has it.
cheap: Pointing at unhappy successful people. Survivorship works both ways.

proposition: Changing your mind often is a sign of good thinking, not weak conviction.
cheap: Praising open-mindedness. Someone who updates on every argument they hear is not thinking well either.

proposition: If you have done nothing wrong you have nothing to fear from surveillance.
cheap: This is the proposition most people reject on sight. Build the strongest version anyway, then see what actually defeats it.

proposition: Long periods alone are necessary for serious thought.
cheap: Listing solitary geniuses. Selection again, and plenty of thinking happens in argument.

proposition: Reading widely is overrated compared with reading a few things repeatedly.
cheap: Saying depth beats breadth. Say how you would know which few things before you have read widely.

proposition: Advice from people who succeeded is nearly worthless.
cheap: Naming survivorship bias and stopping. If it were worthless, apprenticeship would not work.

proposition: Some works of art are objectively better than others.
cheap: Appealing to consensus. Consensus has been wrong, and it varies by era.

proposition: Difficulty in a work of art is usually a defect rather than a virtue.
cheap: Calling it pretentious. That is an accusation about people, not a claim about works.

proposition: What the author meant is irrelevant to what the work means.
cheap: Asserting the intentional fallacy as settled. It is not.

proposition: Modern communication technology has made people worse at sustained thought.
cheap: Citing your own distraction. Every generation has said this about the new medium, and you must answer that.

proposition: A machine that produces good reasoning is doing something that deserves the name thinking.
cheap: Arguing from outputs alone. The Chinese Room is waiting for you.

proposition: Deep specialisation has cost us more than it has gained.
cheap: Romanticising the polymath. Modern medicine is not the work of generalists.

proposition: Life is not obviously better now than a century ago.
cheap: Naming anxiety and loneliness. You have to face the mortality and poverty figures directly.

proposition: Meritocracy is a worse organising principle than it looks.
cheap: Saying merit is partly luck. Now say what should replace it, and why that is better.
